claim: The yeast vacuole plays a positive essential role in initiation of the cell-cycle.
source: Here we present the unexpected finding that the yeast vacuole plays a positive essential role in initiation of the cell-cycle.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the abstract and is supported by experimental data showing cell-cycle arrest in the absence of a functional vacuole.

claim: When vacuole inheritance fails, a new vacuole is generated.
source: When inheritance fails, a new vacuole is generated.
evidence: Supported by FM4-64 pulse-chase experiments showing Vph1-GFP positive structures lacking FM4-64 in daughter cells of vac17Δ mutants.

claim: New vacuole generation occurs prior to the next cell-cycle.
source: We show that this occurs prior to the next cell-cycle, and gain insight into this alternative pathway.
evidence: Demonstrated by measurements showing vacuoles reach a specific size before bud formation in vac17Δ new daughter cells.

claim: A combination of a defect in inheritance with an acute block in vacuole biogenesis results in the loss of a functional vacuole and a specific arrest of cells in early G1 phase.
source: Moreover, we find that a combination of a defect in inheritance with an acute block in the vacuole biogenesis results in the loss of a functional vacuole and a specific arrest of cells in early G1 phase.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing 80% G1 arrest in vac17Δ pep12-60tsf double mutants at restrictive temperature.

claim: The role of the vacuole in cell-cycle progression requires an intact TORC1-SCH9 pathway that can only signal from a mature vacuole.
source: Furthermore, this role for the vacuole in cell-cycle progression requires an intact TORC1-SCH9 pathway that can only signal from a mature vacuole.
evidence: Supported by genetic interactions showing vac17Δ tor1Δ synthetic lethality and rescue by phospho-mimetic sch9-2D3E, plus localization data showing delayed Sch9 recruitment to new vacuoles.

claim: During cell division in budding yeast, the daughter cell inherits a vacuole from the mother cell.
source: During cell division in budding yeast, the daughter cell inherits a vacuole from the mother cell (Weisman et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The vacuole is transported by a vacuole transport complex, composed of the myosin V motor Myo2, the vacuole membrane anchored protein Vac8, and an adaptor protein Vac17 that links Myo2 and Vac8.
source: The vacuole is transported by a vacuole transport complex, composed of the myosin V motor Myo2, the vacuole membrane anchored protein Vac8, and an adaptor protein Vac17 that links Myo2 and Vac8 (Catlett and Weisman, 1998; Wang et al., 1998; Ishikawa et al., 2003; Tang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Vacuole inheritance is initiated in G1 phase via Cdk1/Cdc28, which regulates the formation of the vacuole transport complex.
source: Vacuole inheritance is initiated in G1 phase via Cdk1/Cdc28, which regulates the formation of the vacuole transport complex (Peng and Weisman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: After formation of the complex, Myo2 moves the vacuole to the daughter cell along actin cables.
source: After formation of the complex, Myo2 moves the vacuole to the daughter cell along actin cables (Hill et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: At the end of the cell-cycle, vacuole transport is terminated by ubiquitylation of Vac17, which is then degraded by the 26S proteasome.
source: At the end of the cell-cycle, vacuole transport is terminated by ubiquitylation of Vac17, which is then degraded by the 26S proteasome (Yau et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Myo2 also delivers other cargoes including mitochondria, peroxisomes, secretory vesicles, late-Golgi elements, and astral microtubules.
source: Notably, Myo2 also delivers other cargoes including mitochondria, peroxisomes, secretory vesicles, late-Golgi elements, and astral microtubules.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Myo2 binds to each cargo via cargo specific adaptors, which attach to the globular tail domain of Myo2.
source: Myo2 binds to each cargo via cargo specific adaptors, which attach to the globular tail domain of Myo2 (Yin et al., 2000; Itoh et al., 2002; Boldogh et al., 2004; Itoh et al., 2004; Fagarasanu et al., 2006; Arai et al., 2008; Lipatova et al., 2008; Jin et al., 2011; Santiago-Tirado et al., 2011; Eves et al., 2012; Chernyakov et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Some of the regulatory pathways for vacuole transport are also utilized by other Myo2 cargoes.
source: Moreover, some of the regulatory pathways for vacuole transport are also utilized by other Myo2 cargoes (Moore and Miller, 2007; Peng and Weisman, 2008; Fagarasanu et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2009; Yau et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Many of the proteins involved in vacuole inheritance are conserved among several species, which suggests that vacuole inheritance confers a selective advantage.
source: Many of the proteins involved in vacuole inheritance are conserved among several species, which suggests that vacuole inheritance confers a selective advantage (Mast et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation and inference from conservation data.

claim: Mutations that block vacuole inheritance do not have a notable impact on cell viability.
source: Surprisingly, mutations that block vacuole inheritance do not have a notable impact on cell viability (Catlett and Weisman, 1998; Ishikawa et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies suggest that new vacuole synthesis occurs in the absence of vacuole inheritance.
source: Indeed, previous studies suggest that new vacuole synthesis occurs in the absence of vacuole inheritance (Weisman et al., 1990; Gomes De Mesquita et al., 1997), however at the time of those studies, there were no suitable methods to distinguish an old vacuole from newly formed vacuoles.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work, with acknowledgment of methodological limitations.

claim: Vacuole biogenesis utilizes at least three direct transport pathways: autophagy/Cvt (from the cytoplasm), AP-3/ALP (from the Golgi), and CPY (from the MVB/endosome) pathways.
source: Note that vacuole biogenesis utilizes at least three direct transport pathways: autophagy/Cvt (from the cytoplasm), AP-3/ALP (from the Golgi), and CPY (from the MVB/endosome) pathways (Bryant and Stevens, 1998; Hecht et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In vac17Δ cells, buds contained small Vph1-GFP positive vacuoles that lack FM4-64.
source: Interestingly in vac17Δ, buds contained small Vph1-GFP positive vacuoles that lack FM4-64 (Figure 1A; open white allow heads, see also [Anand et al., 2009]).
evidence: Directly observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There is new vacuole synthesis in the absence of vacuole inheritance, and the new synthesis initiates in the bud.
source: This observation indicates that there is new vacuole synthesis in the absence of vacuole inheritance, and that the new synthesis initiates in the bud.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of Vph1-GFP positive, FM4-64 negative structures in buds of vac17Δ cells.

claim: In wild-type cells, the vacuole is inherited and FM4-64 is distributed between the mother and daughter vacuole.
source: In wild-type cells, the vacuole is inherited and FM4-64 is distributed between the mother and daughter vacuole (Wang et al., 1996), and Vph1-GFP and FM4-64 always colocalize (Figure 1A, top panels).
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments and supported by citation.

claim: In the vac17Δ mutant, FM4-64 is retained in the mother cell.
source: In contrast, in the vacuole inheritance mutant vac17Δ, FM4-64 is retained in the mother cell (Ishikawa et al., 2003).
evidence: Observed in experiments and supported by citation.

claim: In the vac17Δ mutant, the vacuoles grew prior to the generation of a bud.
source: Notably, we found that in the vac17Δ mutant, the vacuoles grew prior to the generation of a bud (Figure 1B, black arrow).
evidence: Demonstrated by measurements of vacuole size relative to cell size in unbudded vs budded cells.

claim: In unbudded new daughters of the vac17Δ mutant, the vacuole diameter relative to cell diameter was smaller than that of wild-type and vac17Δ unbudded old mother cells.
source: In unbudded new daughters of the vac17Δ mutant, the vacuole diameter relative to cell diameter was smaller than that of wild-type and vac17Δ unbudded old mother cells (Figure 1B, left panel).
evidence: Quantified from microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The average diameter of the vacuole was only 5.7(±1.5)% of the cell diameter in new unbudded vac17Δ cells.
source: Notably, the average diameter of the vacuole was only 5.7(±1.5)% of the cell diameter in new unbudded vac17Δ cells.
evidence: Quantified from microscopy measurements.

claim: After production of a small bud, the average mother cell vacuole diameter was 10(±3.8)% of the cell diameter.
source: However, after production of a small bud, the average mother cell vacuole diameter was 10(±3.8)% of the cell diameter.
evidence: Quantified from microscopy measurements.

claim: There was no significant increase in the relative percent diameter of the vacuoles in wild-type and vac17Δ old mother cells with or without a small bud.
source: In contrast, there was no significant increase in the relative percent diameter of the vacuoles in wild-type and vac17Δ old mother cells with or without a small bud.
evidence: Quantified from microscopy measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: The vacuoles in the new daughter cells grow to a minimum size prior to producing a bud.
source: These observations show that the vacuoles in the new daughter cells grow to a minimum size prior to producing a bud.
evidence: Inferred from measurements showing vacuole size increases before bud formation in vac17Δ new cells.

claim: The vacuoles in vac17Δ new mothers continued to grow, and grew faster than vacuoles in either wild-type or vac17Δ old mother cells.
source: Note that the vacuoles in vac17Δ new mothers continued to grow, and grew faster than vacuoles in either wild-type or vac17Δ old mother cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, green line vs the black/pink lines).
evidence: Demonstrated by trend line analysis of vacuole size vs bud size measurements.

claim: Cells actively synthesize new vacuoles in the absence of inherited vacuoles.
source: These observations suggest that cells actively synthesize new vacuoles in the absence of inherited vacuoles, and further suggest that there are mechanisms that regulate vacuole size in proportion to cell size.
evidence: Inferred from growth rate analysis of vacuoles in vac17Δ new cells.

claim: There are mechanisms that regulate vacuole size in proportion to cell size.
source: These observations suggest that cells actively synthesize new vacuoles in the absence of inherited vacuoles, and further suggest that there are mechanisms that regulate vacuole size in proportion to cell size.
evidence: Inferred from observations of proportional vacuole-cell size relationships and differential growth rates.

claim: The average vacuole diameter relative to cell diameter of all the vac17Δ old mother cells was larger than that of wild-type and vac17Δ new mother cells.
source: In addition, the average vacuole diameter relative to cell diameter of all the vac17Δ old mother cells was larger than that of wild-type and vac17Δ new mother cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Quantified from microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Vacuole inheritance is important for regulating vacuole size in the mother cell.
source: This suggests that vacuole inheritance is also important for regulating vacuole size in the mother cell.
evidence: Inferred from observation that vac17Δ old mother cells have larger vacuoles than wild-type.

claim: All vac17Δ mother cells and unbudded cells have a vacuole as defined by the presence of Vph1-GFP.
source: We observed that all vac17Δ mother cells and unbudded cells have a vacuole as defined by the presence of Vph1-GFP.
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments.

claim: The vacuole is required for cell growth and viability.
source: This strongly suggests that the vacuole is required for cell growth and viability.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all cells have a vacuole and from synthetic lethality experiments.

claim: A combination of a vacuole inheritance defect with an additional defect in the synthesis of a new vacuole would render the cell inviable.
source: If this were true, then a combination of a vacuole inheritance defect with an additional defect in the synthesis of a new vacuole would render the cell inviable.
evidence: Logical prediction tested by synthetic lethality experiments.

claim: An additional defect in vacuole function(s) that are required for bud emergence would result in non-viable cells.
source: Similarly, an additional defect in vacuole function(s) that are required for bud emergence would result in non-viable cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Logical prediction illustrated in Figure 2A and tested experimentally.

claim: The double mutants, vac17Δ pep12Δ and vac17Δ vps45Δ displayed synthetic growth defects.
source: We individually tested double mutants of vac17Δ with each of the previously proposed candidates that are not essential genes, and found that the double mutants, vac17Δ pep12Δ and vac17Δ vps45Δ displayed synthetic growth defects (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by tetrad dissection and colony size measurements shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: pep12Δ and vps45Δ were also synthetically lethal with additional mutants defective in vacuole inheritance, vac8Δ and myo2-N1304D mutants.
source: Importantly pep12Δ and vps45Δ were also synthetically lethal with additional mutants defective in vacuole inheritance, vac8Δ and myo2-N1304D mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: PEP12 and VPS45 likely play a critical role in the generation of a new vacuole.
source: The corresponding wild-type genes, PEP12 and VPS45, likely play a critical role in the generation of a new vacuole.
evidence: Inferred from synthetic lethality with vacuole inheritance mutants.

claim: PEP12 encodes a t-SNARE, and VPS45 encodes a Sec1/Munc18 protein.
source: PEP12 encodes a t-SNARE, and VPS45 encodes a Sec1/Munc18 protein.
evidence: Established knowledge about these genes.

claim: PEP12 and VPS45 function together in the vacuole-protein-sorting pathway from endosomes to the vacuole.
source: These proteins function together in the vacuole-protein-sorting pathway from endosomes to the vacuole (Becherer et al., 1996; Burd et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Single pep12Δ cells showed an abnormal distribution of Vph1, but not CMAC.
source: However, single pep12Δ cells, which have a defect in protein sorting to the vacuole, and a partial defect in vacuole inheritance (Raymond et al., 1992), showed an abnormal distribution of Vph1 (Piper et al., 1997), but not CMAC (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2D,E and supported by citations.

claim: The vac17Δ pep12Δ double mutant cells showed defects in the localization of Vph1 and CMAC.
source: The vac17Δ pep12Δ double mutant cells showed defects in the localization of Vph1 and CMAC (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The double mutant does not generate normal vacuoles.
source: These findings suggest that the double mutant does not generate normal vacuoles.
evidence: Inferred from defects in Vph1 and CMAC localization in vac17Δ pep12Δ cells.

claim: In 63% of vac17Δ cells, GFP-Pep12 was present on the newly synthesized vacuole in the bud, which was Vph1-CFP positive but lacked FM4-64.
source: In this strain, 63% of vac17Δ cells had GFP-Pep12 on the newly synthesized vacuole in the bud, which was Vph1-CFP positive but lacked FM4-64 (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Quantified from microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: In 17% of daughter cells, GFP-Pep12 was present in buds without a vacuole, as indicated by the absence of Vph1-CFP.
source: In 17% of daughter cells, GFP-Pep12 was present in buds without a vacuole, as indicated by the absence of Vph1-CFP (vacuole).
evidence: Quantified from microscopy experiments.

claim: A Pep12-positive endosome appears first, and subsequently a Vph1-positive vacuole matures from the Pep12-positive endosome.
source: This suggests that a Pep12-positive endosome appears first, and subsequently a Vph1-positive vacuole matures from the Pep12-positive endosome.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal sequence of GFP-Pep12 and Vph1-CFP appearance in daughter cells.

claim: The vac17Δ pep12-60tsf double mutant, but not pep12-60tsf single mutant, showed a severe growth defect at 37°C.
source: Importantly, the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf double mutant, but not pep12-60tsf single mutant, showed a severe growth defect at 37°C (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: After incubation at 37°C for 24 hr, 80(±3)% of the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf double mutant cells arrested at G1 phase (1N DNA).
source: In contrast, after incubation at the restrictive temperature for 24 hr, 80(±3)% of the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf double mutant cells arrested at G1 phase (1N DNA).
evidence: Quantified from flow cytometry analysis of DNA content.

claim: At 8, 12 and 24 hr after the shift to 37°C, the differences between the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf double mutant and the other strains were statistically significant (all p-values < 1 × 10−3).
source: Importantly, at 8, 12 and 24 hr after the shift to 37°C, the differences between the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf double mutant and the other strains were statistically significant (all p-values < 1 × 10−3).
evidence: Statistical analysis of flow cytometry data.

claim: A functional vacuole is important for cell-cycle progression from G1 phase.
source: These results strongly suggest that a functional vacuole is important for cell-cycle progression from G1 phase.
evidence: Inferred from G1 arrest in vac17Δ pep12Δ and vac17Δ vps45Δ double mutants.

claim: There was a measurable increase in the lethality of the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf mutant.
source: There was a measurable increase in the lethality of the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf mutant.
evidence: Measured by colony formation assays after temperature shift.

claim: The difference between the lethality of the pep12-60tsf single mutant and the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf double mutant was not statistically significant (p = 0.082).
source: However the difference between the lethality of the pep12-60tsf single mutant and the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf double mutant was not statistically significant (p = 0.082) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of lethality data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cells without a functional vacuole arrest at G1 phase, and this arrest is not an artifact of general cell death.
source: Together, these observations strongly suggest that cells without a functional vacuole arrest at G1 phase, and that this arrest is not an artifact of general cell death.
evidence: Inferred from G1 arrest data combined with lethality measurements showing the arrest precedes significant cell death.

claim: When the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf mutant was incubated at the restrictive temperature, there was a striking increase of cells with Whi5 in the nucleus.
source: Additional evidence for a specific arrest in G1 phase, came from the finding that when the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf mutant was incubated at the restrictive temperature, there was a striking increase of cells with Whi5 in the nucleus (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Whi5 is a transcriptional repressor of the SBF complex (Swi4-Swi6), and is localized in the nucleus in early G1 phase.
source: Whi5 is a transcriptional repressor of the SBF complex (Swi4-Swi6), and is localized in the nucleus in early G1 phase (Costanzo et al., 2004; de Bruin et al., 2004).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In wild-type cells, Whi5 nuclear localization is transient and released by Cdc28-Cln3 activity, which enables progression to early G1 phase.
source: In wild-type cells, Whi5 nuclear localization is transient and released by Cdc28-Cln3 activity, which enables progression to early G1 phase.
evidence: Established knowledge about cell-cycle regulation.

claim: After incubation at 37°C for 24 hr, 99% of the G1 cells were unbudded, in both the wild-type and vac17Δ pep12-60tsf mutant.
source: After incubation at 37°C for 24 hr, 99% of the G1 cells were unbudded, in both the wild-type and vac17Δ pep12-60tsf mutant (Figure 3D).
evidence: Quantified from microscopy analysis of flow cytometry-sorted cells shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The vacuole is required for early G1 progression.
source: Together these results indicate that the vacuole is required for early G1 progression.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including G1 arrest, Whi5 localization, and unbudded morphology.

claim: Deletion of Target Of Rapamycin 1 (TOR1) showed synthetic growth defects with vac17Δ and vac8Δ.
source: Evidence for a candidate signaling pathway came from studies which showed that deletion of Target Of Rapamycin 1 (TOR1) showed synthetic growth defects with vac17Δ and vac8Δ (Zurita-Martinez et al., 2007; Costanzo et al., 2010) (Figure 4—fiugre supplements 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by tetrad dissection shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B and supported by citations.

claim: The vacuole inheritance mutant, myo2-N1304D, was synthetic lethal with tor1Δ.
source: Similarly, another vacuole inheritance mutant, myo2-N1304D, was synthetic lethal with tor1Δ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The vac17Δ tor1Δ double mutant showed an increase in cells arrested at G1 phase.
source: Notably, the vac17Δ tor1Δ double mutant showed an increase in cells arrested at G1 phase (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The G1 arrest in vac17Δ tor1Δ was similar to that observed for the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf and vac17Δ pep12Δ mutants.
source: This arrest in G1 phase was similar to that observed for the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf and vac17Δ pep12Δ mutants (Figure 3—figure supplements 1A–C).
evidence: Comparison of flow cytometry data across different mutants.

claim: TORC1 signaling from the vacuole may account at least in part for the G1 arrest observed in the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf and vac17Δ pep12Δ mutants.
source: This suggests that TORC1 signaling from the vacuole may account at least in part for the G1 arrest observed in the vac17Δ pep12-60tsf and vac17Δ pep12Δ mutants.
evidence: Inferred from similarity of G1 arrest phenotypes between vac17Δ tor1Δ and vac17Δ pep12 mutants.

claim: The vac17Δ tor1Δ mutants generated a new vacuole in the daughter cells.
source: Interestingly, the vac17Δ tor1Δ mutants generated a new vacuole in the daughter cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TOR1 functions after the synthesis of the new vacuole.
source: This suggests that TOR1 functions after the synthesis of the new vacuole.
evidence: Inferred from observation that vac17Δ tor1Δ cells can generate new vacuoles but still arrest.

claim: TOR1 encodes a PIK-related protein kinase.
source: TOR1 encodes a PIK-related protein kinase (Alarcon et al., 1999).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In yeast, Tor1 functions in the TORC1 complex, which is composed of Tor1/2, Kog1, Lst8, and Tco89.
source: In yeast, Tor1 functions in the TORC1 complex, which is composed of Tor1/2, Kog1, Lst8, and Tco89 (Loewith et al., 2002).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In yeast, TORC1 localizes on the vacuole membrane.
source: In yeast, TORC1 localizes on the vacuole membrane (Reinke et al., 2004; Araki et al., 2005; Urban et al., 2007; Sturgill et al., 2008; Binda et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2014), and is a key determinant of nutrient status (Di Como and Arndt, 1996).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: TORC1 is a key determinant of nutrient status.
source: In yeast, TORC1 localizes on the vacuole membrane (Reinke et al., 2004; Araki et al., 2005; Urban et al., 2007; Sturgill et al., 2008; Binda et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2014), and is a key determinant of nutrient status (Di Como and Arndt, 1996).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The kinase activity of Tor1 was required for growth of vac17Δ.
source: We found that the kinase activity of Tor1 was required for growth of vac17Δ (Figure 4D), and that the TORC1 specific subunit KOG1 was also required for growth of vac17Δ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by complementation experiments with kinase-dead mutants shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The TORC1 specific subunit KOG1 was required for growth of vac17Δ.
source: We found that the kinase activity of Tor1 was required for growth of vac17Δ (Figure 4D), and that the TORC1 specific subunit KOG1 was also required for growth of vac17Δ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The lst8-15 temperature sensitive mutant is synthetically lethal with vac17Δ.
source: In addition, the lst8-15 temperature sensitive mutant is also synthetically lethal with vac17Δ (Costanzo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The kinase activity of the TORC1 complex is required for normal growth of vacuole inheritance mutants.
source: These results suggest that the kinase activity of the TORC1 complex is required for normal growth of vacuole inheritance mutants.
evidence: Inferred from multiple genetic experiments showing requirement for Tor1 kinase activity, Kog1, and Lst8.

claim: One critical target of TORC1 is the Sch9 kinase, which shares overlapping functions with metazoan S6 kinase.
source: One critical target of TORC1 is the Sch9 kinase, which shares overlapping functions with metazoan S6 kinase (Ballou et al., 1991; Oldham et al., 2000; Christie et al., 2002).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TORC1 directly phosphorylates Sch9 on several serines and threonines.
source: TORC1 directly phosphorylates Sch9 on several serines and threonines, and the phospho-mimetic sch9-2D3E, but not wild-type SCH9 or the Ala-substituted sch9-5A mutant bypasses the TORC1 inhibitor, rapamycin (Loewith et al., 2002; Urban et al., 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The phospho-mimetic sch9-2D3E, but not wild-type SCH9 or the Ala-substituted sch9-5A mutant bypasses the TORC1 inhibitor, rapamycin.
source: TORC1 directly phosphorylates Sch9 on several serines and threonines, and the phospho-mimetic sch9-2D3E, but not wild-type SCH9 or the Ala-substituted sch9-5A mutant bypasses the TORC1 inhibitor, rapamycin (Loewith et al., 2002; Urban et al., 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The phospho-mimetic sch9-2D3E mutant partially suppressed the growth defect of the vac17Δ tor1Δ mutant.
source: Notably, the phospho-mimetic sch9-2D3E mutant partially suppressed the growth defect of the vac17Δ tor1Δ mutant (Figure 4E), suggesting that the arrest of this mutant is due in part to defects in TORC1 mediated signaling via SCH9.
evidence: Demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The arrest of the vac17Δ tor1Δ mutant is due in part to defects in TORC1 mediated signaling via SCH9.
source: Notably, the phospho-mimetic sch9-2D3E mutant partially suppressed the growth defect of the vac17Δ tor1Δ mutant (Figure 4E), suggesting that the arrest of this mutant is due in part to defects in TORC1 mediated signaling via SCH9.
evidence: Inferred from suppression of vac17Δ tor1Δ growth defect by sch9-2D3E.

claim: Sch9-2D3E localizes on the vacuole membrane.
source: It was previously shown that Sch9-2D3E localizes on the vacuole membrane (Urban et al., 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: sch9-2D3E did not suppress the vac17Δ pep12Δ double mutant.
source: Notably sch9-2D3E did not suppress the vac17Δ pep12Δ double mutant (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A functional vacuole is required for the roles of the TORC1-SCH9 pathway in cell-cycle progression from G1 phase.
source: This suggests that a functional vacuole is required for the roles of the TORC1-SCH9 pathway in cell-cycle progression from G1 phase.
evidence: Inferred from the inability of sch9-2D3E to suppress vac17Δ pep12Δ despite suppressing vac17Δ tor1Δ.

claim: TORC1 signals from the vacuole/lysosome.
source: While previous studies showed that TORC1 signals from the vacuole/lysosome (Sancak et al., 2010), and that Sch9 is activated in that location (Urban et al., 2007), it was assumed that once Sch9 is activated, it no longer requires the vacuole for its further downstream functions.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sch9 is activated on the vacuole/lysosome.
source: While previous studies showed that TORC1 signals from the vacuole/lysosome (Sancak et al., 2010), and that Sch9 is activated in that location (Urban et al., 2007), it was assumed that once Sch9 is activated, it no longer requires the vacuole for its further downstream functions.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The vacuole is required for Sch9 function(s) after Sch9 is phosphorylated by TORC1.
source: However our findings strongly suggest that the vacuole is required for Sch9 function(s) after Sch9 is phosphorylated by TORC1.
evidence: Inferred from the inability of phospho-mimetic sch9-2D3E to suppress vac17Δ pep12Δ.

claim: Target protein(s) of the Sch9 kinase may need to be present on the vacuole membrane.
source: One possible role of the vacuole in Sch9 function, is that target protein(s) of the Sch9 kinase must be present on the vacuole membrane.
evidence: Speculative explanation for why Sch9 requires a functional vacuole.

claim: The full kinase activity of Sch9 may require other proteins that are on the vacuole membrane.
source: Alternatively or in addition, the full kinase activity of Sch9 may require other proteins that are on the vacuole membrane.
evidence: Speculative explanation for why Sch9 requires a functional vacuole.

claim: In vac17Δ cells, GFP-Sch9 was defective in its localization to the new vacuoles, while the localization of Tor1 and Kog1 were unaffected.
source: Notably, in vac17Δ cells, GFP-Sch9 was defective in its localization to the new vacuoles, while the localization of Tor1 and Kog1 were unaffected (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Sch9 recruitment to the newly formed vacuole is slower than the recruitment of Vph1 and Tor1.
source: These analyses show that Sch9 recruitment to the newly formed vacuole is slower than the recruitment of Vph1 and Tor1.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of fluorescence signals in buds of different sizes.

claim: Small budded cells did not have fluorescent signals for Vph1, Tor1, or Sch9, indicating that these small buds do not have a vacuole.
source: Specifically, small budded cells did not have fluorescent signals for any of the proteins, which indicates that these small buds do not have a vacuole (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 5C–F.

claim: As the bud increases in size, in most cases, Vph1-CFP and Tor1-3xGFP appeared simultaneously.
source: As the bud increases in size, in most cases, Vph1-CFP and Tor1-3xGFP appeared simultaneously (Figure 5C).
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Tor1-3xGFP is immediately recruited to the newly formed vacuoles.
source: This indicates that Tor1-3xGFP is immediately recruited to the newly formed vacuoles.
evidence: Inferred from simultaneous appearance of Vph1-CFP and Tor1-3xGFP.

claim: In some small budded cells, Tor1-3xGFP was present without Vph1-CFP, which suggests that Tor1 may be present at endosomes in these small budded cells.
source: Moreover in some small budded cells, Tor1-3xGFP was present without Vph1-CFP, which suggests that Tor1 may be present at endosomes in these small budded cells.
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments and interpreted based on known endosome-to-vacuole pathway.

claim: In medium sized buds (0.62(±0.14) daughter size/mother size) only Vph1-CFP is present without GFP-Sch9.
source: In medium sized buds (0.62(±0.14) daughter size/mother size) only Vph1-CFP is present.
evidence: Quantified from microscopy measurements.

claim: The average bud size where both Vph1 and Sch9 are present is 0.79(±0.11).
source: The average bud size where both Vph1 and Sch9 are present is 0.79(±0.11).
evidence: Quantified from microscopy measurements.

claim: Sch9 recruitment is delayed compared to Vph1 and Tor1, but eventually occurs.
source: Thus Sch9 recruitment is delayed compared to Vph1 and Tor1, but eventually occurs.
evidence: Inferred from temporal analysis of fluorescence signals in buds of different sizes.

claim: The recruitment of the Sch9-2D3E mutant was similar to the recruitment of wild-type Sch9.
source: Notably the recruitment of the Sch9-2D3E mutant was similar to the recruitment of wild-type Sch9 (Figure 5E), indicating that the growth suppression of the vac17Δ tor1Δ mutant by sch9-2D3E is not due to a faster recruitment to the vacuole.
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The growth suppression of the vac17Δ tor1Δ mutant by sch9-2D3E is not due to a faster recruitment to the vacuole.
source: Notably the recruitment of the Sch9-2D3E mutant was similar to the recruitment of wild-type Sch9 (Figure 5E), indicating that the growth suppression of the vac17Δ tor1Δ mutant by sch9-2D3E is not due to a faster recruitment to the vacuole.
evidence: Inferred from similar recruitment kinetics of Sch9 and Sch9-2D3E.

claim: PI(3,5)P2, an inositol lipid which is present at the vacuole membrane, is required for vacuole membrane targeting of Sch9.
source: PI(3,5)P2, an inositol lipid which is present at the vacuole membrane, is required for vacuole membrane targeting of Sch9 (Jin et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The timing of the recruitment of Fab1 was similar to that observed for Sch9.
source: Notably the timing of the recruitment of Fab1 was similar to that observed for Sch9.
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments.

claim: In a vac17Δ mutant which co-expressed Vph1-CFP and Fab1-3xGFP, only Vph1-CFP is present in medium buds (approximately 0.6 daughter size/mother size).
source: In a vac17Δ mutant which co-expressed Vph1-CFP and Fab1-3xGFP, only Vph1-CFP is present in medium buds (approximately 0.6 daughter size/mother size) (Figure 5F).
evidence: Observed in microscopy experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The average bud size where both Vph1 and Fab1 are present was 0.76(±0.10).
source: The average bud size where both Vph1 and Fab1 are present was 0.76(±0.10).
evidence: Quantified from microscopy measurements.

claim: Fab1 recruitment is delayed compared to Tor1, but is similar to that observed for Sch9.
source: Thus Fab1 recruitment is delayed compared to Tor1, but is similar to that observed for Sch9.
evidence: Inferred from temporal analysis of fluorescence signals.

claim: There are differences between new vacuoles and inherited vacuoles.
source: These observations suggest that there are differences between new vacuoles and inherited vacuoles, and that the newly synthesized vacuoles are missing specific components of mature vacuoles that are essential for cell-cycle progression.
evidence: Inferred from differential recruitment kinetics of vacuolar proteins.

claim: The newly synthesized vacuoles are missing specific components of mature vacuoles that are essential for cell-cycle progression.
source: These observations suggest that there are differences between new vacuoles and inherited vacuoles, and that the newly synthesized vacuoles are missing specific components of mature vacuoles that are essential for cell-cycle progression.
evidence: Inferred from delayed recruitment of Sch9 and Fab1 to new vacuoles.

claim: A functional vacuole is crucial for cell-cycle progression at G1 phase.
source: Together, these observations demonstrate that a functional vacuole is crucial for cell-cycle progression at G1 phase, and that the TORC1-SCH9 pathway is part of this critical function (Figure 4G).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The TORC1-SCH9 pathway is part of the critical function of the vacuole in cell-cycle progression.
source: Together, these observations demonstrate that a functional vacuole is crucial for cell-cycle progression at G1 phase, and that the TORC1-SCH9 pathway is part of this critical function (Figure 4G).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic and localization studies.

claim: TORC1-SCH9 signaling from the vacuole may be involved in G1 progression through its known functions in ribosome biogenesis and translation.
source: TORC1-SCH9 signaling from the vacuole may be involved in G1 progression through its known functions in a ribosome biogenesis and translation (Barbet et al., 1996; Jorgensen et al., 2004; Urban et al., 2007).
evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citations to known TORC1-SCH9 functions.

claim: The TORC1-SCH9 pathway may signal the cell-cycle machinery that a functional vacuole is present and hence the cell is ready to progress from G1.
source: Alternatively, the TORC1-SCH9 pathway may signal the cell-cycle machinery that a functional vacuole is present and hence the cell is ready to progress from G1.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed based on experimental findings.

claim: Sch9 activity is critical for cell size.
source: Previous studies showed that Sch9 activity is critical for cell size (Jorgensen et al., 2004; Urban et al., 2007), and that cell size correlates with vacuole size (Chan and Marshall, 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cell size correlates with vacuole size.
source: Previous studies showed that Sch9 activity is critical for cell size (Jorgensen et al., 2004; Urban et al., 2007), and that cell size correlates with vacuole size (Chan and Marshall, 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TORC1-SCH9 localization and signaling from the vacuole is critical for the regulation of cell size.
source: These observations together with the current study suggest that TORC1-SCH9 localization and signaling from the vacuole is critical for the regulation of cell size.
evidence: Inferred from current findings combined with previous knowledge about Sch9 and cell size.

claim: An analogous regulation of the cell-cycle may occur from endo-lysosomal membranes in other organisms.
source: It is tempting to speculate that an analogous regulation of the cell-cycle occurs from endo-lysosomal membranes in other organisms.
evidence: Speculative extrapolation of findings to other organisms.

claim: Cells possess novel checkpoint mechanisms that prevent cell-cycle progression at G1 phase in the absence of essential organelles.
source: In addition, these findings lead to the hypothesis that cells possess novel checkpoint mechanisms that prevent cell-cycle progression at G1 phase in the absence of essential organelles.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed based on experimental findings.

claim: Vacuoles were detected using GFP fused to the integral vacuole membrane protein Vph1, a V0 subunit of the vacuolar ATPase.
source: Vacuoles were detected using GFP fused to the integral vacuole membrane protein Vph1, a V0 subunit of the vacuolar ATPase (Manolson et al., 1992).
evidence: Methodological approach supported by citation.

claim: The presence of inherited vacuoles or old vacuoles were specifically assessed via pulse chase experiments with the vital fluorophore FM4-64.
source: The presence of inherited vacuoles or old vacuoles were specifically assessed via pulse chase experiments with the vital fluorophore FM4-64 (Vida and Emr, 1995).
evidence: Methodological approach supported by citation.

claim: Exogenously added FM4-64 binds to the plasma membrane, is internalized by endocytosis and delivered to the vacuole.
source: Exogenously added FM4-64 binds to the plasma membrane, is internalized by endocytosis and delivered to the vacuole.
evidence: Established knowledge about FM4-64 properties.

claim: After a chase of one doubling time, all of the FM4-64 is trapped on the vacuole membrane.
source: After a chase of one doubling time, all of the FM4-64 is trapped on the vacuole membrane.
evidence: Established methodological knowledge about FM4-64 labeling.

claim: In wild-type cells, the vacuole diameter showed a linear relationship with cell diameter.
source: In wild-type cells, the vacuole diameter showed a linear relationship with cell diameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Vacuole volume correlates with cell volume.
source: This is consistent with a previous study that demonstrated that vacuole volume correlates with cell volume (Chan and Marshall, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fab1 is the sole lipid kinase that generates PI(3,5)P2.
source: To test whether the delay in Sch9 recruitment might be due to a delay in the generation of PI(3,5)P2 on newly formed vacuoles, we tested the timing of the recruitment of Fab1, the sole lipid kinase that generates PI(3,5)P2 (Gary et al., 1998).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.
